doc.title: Don Wolff interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 13, 1996

title: Staying with big bands and standards, Tin Pan Alley
summary: Wolff stayed with big bands and mainstream jazz, mixes early and late versions of songs, and loves Tin Pan Alley standards.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Listening to classical music, then and now

blocks.x: Have you been a fan of this music since you were growing up?

Yes. I was a product of the era when everybody else went to Elvis and the Beatles. And I stayed with the big bands, and I stayed with Ellington and Basie and I never moved off of mainstream jazz. Rhythm and melody. I really like the standards. Even the new jazz is really not so much my preference as it is to hear a Gershwin or a Berlin or an Ellington or a Basie tune and hear it done the original way as well as hearing it done today. And I do a lot of that. I call it mixing and matching. Doing the same song done by two different groups or the same performer early in the career and late in the career — nothing more enjoyable than listening to Billie Holiday at the beginning of her career and at the end of her career and listening to the difference in the sounds and the feeling that the woman had during her lifetime.

I’ve often wondered if we are writing, since the ‘40s especially, is anybody writing standards since then you know? In fact Herbie Hancock just came out with a record and I forget the exact title of it, but what he did was he found what he thought were going to be the standards to come. And he did some more modern tunes but treated them as jazz tunes I guess.

Well I think those probably will be standards for our children and maybe our grand- children, but I think for me, certainly for me personally as well as for me collectively, the Tin Pan Alley songs are what America is all about. Those will always be loved songs because they’re just part of America. © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-
